steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on scene flow estimation for LiDAR point clouds. It should motivate a distillation approach that is fast and needs no human labels, contrast it with existing optimization-based and supervised feedforward methods, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why scene flow matters: open-world detection and tracking; examples of current use
- Strengths and weaknesses of the two classes of methods (supervised feedforward vs test-time optimization)
- Our proposal: Scene Flow via Distillation (SFvD) and ZeroFlow
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why scene flow matters
  - important primitive for open-world object detection and tracking
  - example: supervisory boxes for open-world LiDAR detector via offline object extraction, using scene flow from Neural Scene Flow Prior (NSFP)
  - NSFP: no human supervision, but tens of seconds per full-size point cloud pair
  - if NSFP were high quality AND real-time -> runtime primitive in the downstream detector, not just offline pipeline
  - similar: scene flow from FlowNet3D as input primitive for multi-object tracking pipeline
  - FlowNet3D fast enough online on subsampled point clouds, but supervised feedforward -> needs lots of in-domain human annotations
- Two classes of methods
  - supervised feedforward: human annotations, expensive
  - annotations done on consecutive observations to amortize cost -> limited structural diversity (e.g. 15 second AV sequence ~ single city block)
  - large-scale labels rarely available outside AV domains
  - test-time optimization: no labels (hand-built priors), but too slow for online use
- Proposal
  - SFvD: simple, scalable distillation framework; label-free optimization method makes pseudo-labels to supervise feedforward model
  - new class of methods: strengths of both + data scale and diversity -> fast run-time, superior accuracy, no human supervision
  - instantiated as Zero-Label Scalable Scene Flow (ZeroFlow): family of methods, full-size point clouds, high quality estimates
  - results on Argoverse 2 and Waymo Open; state-of-the-art on Argoverse 2 Self-Supervised Scene Flow Challenge (Figure 1)
- Contributions
  - SFvD framework; beats slow optimization methods at feedforward speed
  - ZeroFlow: over 1000x faster than state-of-the-art optimization (29.33 ms ZeroFlow 1X vs 35,281.4 ms Chodosh); over 1000x cheaper to train than human annotation ($394 vs ~$750,000)
  - release pseudo-labels (7.1 GPU months of compute) for Argoverse 2 and Waymo Open, plus code and model weights

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Scene flow estimation is an important building block for open-world object detection and tracking. For example, one prior work uses offline object extraction with high quality scene flow from Neural Scene Flow Prior (NSFP)  to generate supervisory boxes for an open-world LiDAR detector. NSFP does not need human supervision, but it takes tens of seconds to run on one full-size point cloud pair. If NSFP was high quality and also real-time, then its estimates could be used directly as a runtime primitive in the downstream detector, instead of only being used in an offline pipeline. This is similar to how another work uses scene flow from FlowNet3D  as an input primitive for a multi-object tracking pipeline. FlowNet3D is fast enough to run online on subsampled point clouds, but it is a supervised feedforward method, so it needs a lot of in-domain human annotations.

These examples show the strengths and weaknesses of their whole class of approach. Supervised feedforward methods need human annotations, and these are expensive to get. To amortize the cost, annotation is usually done on consecutive observations, and this severely limits the structural diversity of the scenes that get annotated (e.g. a 15 second sequence from an Autonomous Vehicle typically only covers a single city block). Also, because of the cost and how hard labeling is, large-scale labels are rarely available at all outside of Autonomous Vehicle domains. Test-time optimization methods don't need human labels because they rely on hand-built priors, but they are too slow for online scene flow estimation.

We propose Scene Flow via Distillation (SFvD). It is a simple and scalable distillation framework where a label-free optimization method produces pseudo-labels, and these are used to supervise a feedforward model. SFvD gives a new class of scene flow methods that combine the strengths of optimization-based and feedforward methods together with the power of data scale and diversity, so they get fast run-time and better accuracy with no human supervision. We instantiate this pipeline as Zero-Label Scalable Scene Flow (ZeroFlow). ZeroFlow is a family of methods, motivated by real-world applications, that can process full-size point clouds and give high quality scene flow estimates. We show the strength of ZeroFlow on Argoverse 2  and Waymo Open, and in particular it achieves state-of-the-art on the Argoverse 2 Self-Supervised Scene Flow Challenge (Figure 1).

Our main contributions are:

- We introduce Scene Flow via Distillation (SFvD), a simple but effective distillation framework that uses a label-free optimization method to make pseudo-labels that supervise a feedforward model. This lets us beat the performance of slow optimization-based approaches while running at the speed of feedforward methods.

- Using SFvD we present Zero-Label Scalable Scene Flow (ZeroFlow), a family of methods that give fast, state-of-the-art scene flow on full-size clouds. The methods run over 1000 \times faster than state-of-the-art optimization methods on real point clouds (29.33 ms for ZeroFlow 1X vs 35,281.4 ms for Chodosh) and are over 1000 \times cheaper to train than paying for human annotations ($394 vs \sim $750,000).

- We release high quality flow pseudo-labels for the popular Argoverse 2  and Waymo Open  autonomous vehicle datasets, which took 7.1 GPU months of compute, together with our code and trained model weights, to help further research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Scene flow estimation is an important primitive for open-world object detection and tracking [1,2,3,4,5]. For example, [1] generates supervisory boxes for an open-world LiDAR detector through offline object extraction, using high quality scene flow estimates from Neural Scene Flow Prior (NSFP) [6]. While NSFP does not require human supervision, it takes tens of seconds to run on a single full-size point cloud pair. If NSFP were both high quality and real-time, its estimates could be used directly as a runtime primitive in the downstream detector rather than being relegated to an offline pipeline. This runtime formulation is similar to [2]'s use of scene flow from FlowNet3D [7] as an input primitive for their multi-object tracking pipeline; although FlowNet3D is fast enough for online processing of subsampled point clouds, its supervised feedforward formulation requires significant in-domain human annotations.

Broadly, these methods are representative of the strengths and weaknesses of their class of approach. Supervised feedforward methods rely on human annotations, which are expensive. To amortize these costs, annotations are typically made on consecutive observations, which severely limits the structural diversity of the annotated scenes (e.g. a 15 second sequence from an Autonomous Vehicle typically only covers a single city block); because of cost and labeling difficulty, large-scale labels are also rarely available outside of Autonomous Vehicle domains. Test-time optimization techniques avoid the need for human labels by relying on hand-built priors, but they are too slow for online scene flow estimation.

We propose Scene Flow via Distillation (SFvD), a simple, scalable distillation framework that uses a label-free optimization method to produce pseudo-labels for supervising a feedforward model. SFvD yields a new class of scene flow estimation methods that combine the strengths of optimization-based and feedforward methods with the power of data scale and diversity, achieving fast run-time and superior accuracy without human supervision. We instantiate this pipeline as Zero-Label Scalable Scene Flow (ZeroFlow), a family of methods that, motivated by real-world applications, can process full-size point clouds while providing high quality scene flow estimates. We demonstrate the strength of ZeroFlow on Argoverse 2 [8] and Waymo Open [10], notably achieving state-of-the-art on the Argoverse 2 Self-Supervised Scene Flow Challenge (Figure 1).

Our primary contributions are:

- We introduce a simple yet effective distillation framework, Scene Flow via Distillation (SFvD), which uses a label-free optimization method to produce pseudo-labels that supervise a feedforward model, letting us surpass the performance of slow optimization-based approaches at the speed of feedforward methods.

- Using SFvD, we present Zero-Label Scalable Scene Flow (ZeroFlow), a family of methods that produce fast, state-of-the-art scene flow on full-size clouds, running over 1000 \times faster than state-of-the-art optimization methods (29.33 ms for ZeroFlow 1X vs 35,281.4 ms for Chodosh) on real point clouds while being over 1000 \times cheaper to train than human annotations ($394 vs \sim $750,000).

- We release high quality flow pseudo-labels (representing 7.1 GPU months of compute) for the popular Argoverse 2 [8] and Waymo Open [10] autonomous vehicle datasets, along with our code and trained model weights, to facilitate further research.
